sentences.speaker: Dr. Nova
sentences.text: Welcome to Simulator 7.3 Tab A: Continuous Score Divergence and Wasserstein Optimal Transport Studio. Drag the Privileged Mean Shift slider to adjust Delta mu, and move the decision threshold cutoff tau to observe live variations in Wasserstein-1 distance, Kolmogorov-Smirnov gap, and Disparate Impact Ratio.

sentences.speaker: Kaito
sentences.text: Let's test optimal transport interactively! Try sliding the Mean Shift down toward zero to restore distributional parity, or shift the decision cutoff tau higher into the tail to see how severe adverse impact explodes!

sentences.speaker: Dr. Nova
sentences.text: Let us verify your command of distributional metrics in Active Checkpoint 1. In automated credit or hiring systems where decisions occur strictly in the upper tail, why does the Kolmogorov-Smirnov statistic fail to capture severe demographic bias compared to the Wasserstein-1 Earth Mover distance?

sentences.speaker: Kaito
sentences.text: Here is Checkpoint 1! Remember the geometry of the Cumulative Distribution Function versus quantile integration. Choose the option that explains why KS goes blind in the top tail!

sentences.speaker: Dr. Nova
sentences.text: Correct! Kolmogorov-Smirnov measures only the single maximum vertical difference between CDFs, which is bounded by the total probability mass in the upper tail. Wasserstein-1 integrates the horizontal point distance across all quantiles, directly capturing severe horizontal exclusion in high-scoring regions.

sentences.speaker: Dr. Nova
sentences.text: Incorrect. The failure of D sub KS in upper-tail exclusion stems purely from its vertical geometry: a five percent upper tail limits the vertical CDF gap to at most 0.05, whereas Wasserstein-1 integrates the wide horizontal score separation across quantiles.

sentences.speaker: Dr. Nova
sentences.text: Welcome to Simulator 7.3 Tab B: Non-Parametric Permutation Resampling and Power Studio. Here, one thousand Monte Carlo permutations generate an exact empirical null distribution. Try decreasing the unprivileged sample size n zero toward fifteen while holding true disparity constant at 0.08 to observe statistical power collapse live.

sentences.speaker: Kaito
sentences.text: Time to explore permutation resampling! Watch how shrinking the minority subgroup sample size stretches out the null histogram, swallowing genuine algorithmic unfairness and risking a catastrophic Type II error!

sentences.speaker: Dr. Nova
sentences.text: Let us test your auditing rigor in Active Checkpoint 2. An audit evaluates a minority cohort of just sixteen applicants with a 25 percent selection rate versus 45 percent for majority applicants, yielding a severe Disparate Impact Ratio of 0.55. Yet a Z-test gives p equals 0.118. What is the valid conclusion?

sentences.speaker: Kaito
sentences.text: Think carefully about statistical power in Checkpoint 2! Don't let an underpowered p-value trick you into declaring a severely discriminatory system fair!

sentences.speaker: Dr. Nova
sentences.text: Correct! With only sixteen minority applicants, the two-proportion test is severely underpowered. Concluding the model is compliant solely because p exceeds 0.05 commits a dangerous Type II error. Responsible auditors always report logarithmic confidence intervals and minimum detectable effect sizes.

sentences.speaker: Dr. Nova
sentences.text: Incorrect. Failing to reject the null hypothesis when n zero equals sixteen does not prove fairness. The Disparate Impact Ratio of 0.55 reveals severe practical disparity masked by huge sampling variance; declaring parity commits a fatal Type II error.
